title: Throughput & KV Strategy — concurrency caps, prefetching, eviction, and int4 tuning
summary: Deep technical session focusing on throughput tuning options: concurrency caps (max_num_seqs), token ceilings, KV cache prefetch and eviction strategies, and quantization trade-offs (int8 vs int4). Discussed on-prem NIC implications and a concrete benchmark/test plan with next steps.
transcript:
[00:00] Maya Chen (Redwood AE): Hey everyone, thanks for joining. We'll run through concurrency caps, kv cache prefetch/eviction and quant tradeoffs, and sketch a benchmark plan. Diego will lead the deep perf bits.
[00:18] Diego Ramos (Redwood SE): Hi, hi. Quick agenda: 1) continuous batching behavior under peaky load, 2) scheduler knobs — "max_num_seqs", token_limit, concurrency caps, 3) KV cache prefetch and eviction heuristics, 4) quantization impact on throughput/latency, 5) on-prem/VPC network considerations.
[00:40] Ava Patel (Aurora): Sounds good. Our big pain is sudden bursts from our search autocomplete — latency spikes, cost upset, and we want predictable tail latency.
[00:51] Liam O'Connor (Aurora): Also interested in pushing int4 to reduce GPU mem, but worried about quality regression for long-form completions.
[01:05] Diego: Right. On continuous batching, the runtime uses a sliding window to assemble sequences. Default behavior packs short requests to fill max_num_seqs. If you set max_num_seqs too high it can increase latency tail when bursts are sparse.
[01:25] Priya Nair (Aurora): Can you clarify "max_num_seqs" — is that per GPU or per slot? Sometimes our terminology differs.
[01:33] Diego: Good call. In Redwood's scheduler it's per serving instance (per worker) — so per GPU process. So the effective concurrency is max_num_seqs * number_of_workers.
[01:45] Maya: And there's an adaptive circuit that will cap packing window based on SLOs so it won't always wait the max time.
[01:55] Liam: We've seen our own heuristics — adding a short token limit helps prevent long generations from blocking. Is that the token_limit knob?
[02:05] Diego: Yes. token_limit or per-request token_ceiling. If you set token_limit to 128 for interactive flows, a single long job won't steal the slot for hundreds of tokens.
[02:18] Ava: So recommended pattern for our autocomplete would be low token_limit, medium max_num_seqs?
[02:25] Diego: Exactly. For high qps short responses: max_num_seqs 24-32, token_limit 16-64 depending on typical reply length. But depends on model size and batch packing efficiency.
[02:40] Priya: What about prefetching the KV cache — we deploy a reranker and a prompt preface, and cold cache penalties are brutal on tail.
[02:50] Diego: Two things: prefix caching (static prompt + few tokens) and KV warmstart. Redwoods runtime supports a prefetch window — you can configure kv_prefetch_ms to proactively load KV for hot keys when a session is resumed or when pipelined requests are incoming.
[03:05] Maya: We typically recommend kv_prefetch_ms 50-200ms depending on NIC and model. On 100Gb NICs you can push lower; on 25Gb give it more headroom.
[03:18] Liam: Does prefetch increase throughput or just reduce tail latency?
[03:22] Diego: Mostly tail latency — you remove the first-token cold-start hit. But if your workload reuses prefixes heavily, it also reduces compute (since you can reuse KV across requests) which increases effective throughput under sustained load.
[03:35] Ava: Eviction — how aggressive should we be on on-prem? We have limited GPU mem and want high hit rate. What's the trade-off?
[03:44] Diego: Eviction policy is LRU by default, but you can tune to size-based eviction, pinning (for pinned sessions), and time-to-live for ephemeral prompts. For on-prem with limited mem, pin the hottest few prefixes and set aggressive eviction for the rest, then pair with higher prefetch to mitigate misses.
[03:59] Priya: Pinning sounds useful for our heavy enterprise accounts. Is that supported in private deployments?
[04:05] Diego: Yes — Private and Dedicated both support prefix pinning and VPC-level prewarm hooks. For on-prem, we also expose APIs to pre-populate KV at deployment time.
[04:15] Liam: Quantization: int8 vs int4 — what's the performance delta vs quality?
[04:21] Diego: On our benchmarks int8 gives 1.6-1.9x throughput improvement vs fp16 with small to no quality regression. Int4 can give 2.8-3.5x but quality drop varies by model and prompt length. We suggest A/B evals on your prompt set. Also quantization interacts with KV cache size and tokenization because smaller weights mean more tokens can fit in cache but can also amplify hallucination risk on some models.
[04:45] Ava: So we'd run a quant eval on our canonical prompts. Any recommended metric?
[04:49] Maya: Use your NLG metric (BLEU/ROUGE questionable) and human evals for hallucination rate. Redwood Optimize can run blind A/B with same seeds and report diff scores.
[04:59] Priya: On VPC/on-prem networking: what about throughput when model shards cross NICs, and when KV cache traffic gets heavy?
[05:07] Diego: Good question. For model shards we co-locate shards on the same host when possible; if cross-host NVLink is unavailable, GPU-to-GPU over RDMA/100Gb has higher latency. KV cache is in-process memory for many configs; when using remote KV (shared across hosts) you'll need 100Gb to keep tail low. For your planned rack (4x80GB A100s on 100Gb), we expect good results. For 25Gb, you'll likely need more prefetch and slightly lower max_num_seqs to avoid network stalls.
[05:35] Ava: Our on-prem will initially be 25Gb. So maybe we start conservative.
[05:40] Diego: Yes. Start with lower max_num_seqs per worker (16), higher kv_prefetch_ms (150-250ms), and run load tests to observe queueing.
[05:51] Liam: Can we run a microbenchmark that varies three axes: max_num_seqs, kv_prefetch_ms, quant mode?
[05:58] Diego: Absolutely. That's what I want to propose as the test matrix. Suggested grid: max_num_seqs [12, 16, 24, 32], kv_prefetch_ms [50, 150, 300], quant [fp16, int8, int4]. Run each combo with 30-minute steady-state and 10-minute peaky bursts (2x qps) to check tail behavior.
[06:20] Priya: 30 minutes each — that's a lot of time. Can we reduce permutations?
[06:25] Maya: We'll prioritize combos: first narrow quant to fp16 vs int8 for whole matrix, then test int4 on promising configs only.
[06:32] Diego: Also limit to two worker counts to simulate scaling: single worker and 4-worker pool. That reduces total runs.
[06:40] Ava: What metrics should we capture in the run?
[06:44] Diego: P50/P90/P99 latency for generation, tail token latency, token throughput (tokens/sec), GPU util, KV hit rate, memory pressure, and network egress. Also capture per-token cost estimate and quality diffs for quant runs.
[06:58] Liam: Any gotchas about continuous batching warmups? We see a weird mid-run drop where throughput falls for a few minutes.
[07:06] Diego: Possibly due to garbage collection in host process or eviction pressure causing repeated KV reloads. We'll instrument the scheduler windows and gc cycles. Also check for token-ceiling enforcement causing many small batches that blow up overhead.
[07:20] Priya: For security/compliance we need audit logs when pinning prefixes; do those appear in Redwood Private?
[07:27] Maya: Yes, KMS/HSM and audit logs for KV operations are supported in Private with retention settings. We'll include the security doc in follow-ups.
[07:36] Ava: Okay, concrete next steps?
[07:39] Diego: I'll draft the test matrix and a step-by-step runbook. Maya will share the security checklist and the benchmark spreadsheet. You (Aurora) will confirm a node image and network config for on-prem.
[07:50] Liam: We'll provide sample prompt sets and traffic shape. Also we can grant access to a reduced test cluster if helpful.
[07:57] Maya: Great. Any blockers on timeline?
[08:00] Priya: We can start in two weeks when infra slot opens.
[08:03] Maya: Perfect. We'll aim to deliver an initial run plan by Friday next week.
[08:10] Ava: A few more quick clarifying q's?
[08:12] Diego: Sure.
[08:13] Ava: If we pin a prefix, does it consume GPU memory permanently?
[08:16] Diego: Yes, pinned prefixes occupy KV memory until unpinned; that's why we recommend pin only the hottest 5-10 for limited mem.
[08:24] Liam: When you said "adaptive circuit" earlier — is that an automatic fallback to smaller batches when SLOs degrade?
[08:30] Diego: Exactly. The scheduler monitors latency SLOs and will reduce packing window and drop opportunistic batching to favor immediate dispatch. It's tunable per-route.
[08:39] Priya: Any suggested observability thresholds?
[08:41] Maya: Set an alert if P99 > SLA + 20% for two consecutive windows, and KV hit rate < 85% sustained for 5 minutes.
[08:51] Ava: Good. That should help detect regressions quickly.
[08:54] Diego: Also add a synthetic probe that exercises long form to catch token-ceiling regressions.
[08:59] Liam: About quant quality tests — are there tooling hooks to diff traces token-by-token?
[09:03] Diego: Redwood Optimize supports token-level diffs, and you can export side-by-side generations for human review. We'll include instructions.
[09:12] Maya: Ok to recap and action items.
[09:15] Diego: Quick recap: recommended baseline for 25Gb on-prem: max_num_seqs=16, token_limit short for interactive flows, kv_prefetch_ms=150-250ms, pin top prefixes, run grid with fp16/int8 then int4 if safe.
[09:30] Maya: Next steps and owners we captured in the doc. Anything else?
[09:34] Priya: No, that's it. Thanks.
[09:36] Ava: Thanks everyone.
[09:38] Liam: Thanks.
[09:40] Maya: We'll send notes and the bench spreadsheet. Bye.
[09:43] END OF RECORDING
